To corrode means to gradually eat away and destroy a material — usually from the surface inward — through a chemical reaction.

The key ideas packed into this one word are:

  • Gradual — it does not happen suddenly. It takes time, sometimes a very long time.
  • Eating away — something is being worn down, weakened, and slowly destroyed.
  • Chemical reaction — a substance like water, oxygen, acid, or salt reacts with the material and breaks it apart at a molecular level.
The Mental Picture

Imagine leaving an iron nail outside in the rain for a few weeks. You come back, and the nail has a reddish-brown, flaky, rough coating — rust. That nail has been corroded. The water and oxygen in the air reacted with the iron and converted the solid, strong metal into a crumbling, weakened substance.

The destruction did not happen all at once like breaking. It crept in slowly, silently, from the outside — like something being eaten from the surface inward.
Two Ways the Verb is Used

Corrode works both as a transitive verb (acting on something else) and as an intransitive verb (describing something happening to the subject itself).

Transitive — something corrodes something else:

"The acid corroded the metal pipes."
"Saltwater corrodes iron at a much faster rate than fresh water."
"The chemicals in the soil had slowly corroded the buried cables."

Here, the acid, saltwater, or chemicals are the agents doing the corroding.

Intransitive — something corrodes on its own (or the cause is not stated):

"The iron fence had begun to corrode."
"Without a protective coating, the metal will corrode."
"The copper roof corroded over decades, turning green."

Both uses are equally correct and common.
What Corrodes What? (Common Contexts)

While the concept of corrosion is broad, you will encounter "corrode" most often in these pairings:

  • Metals are the most classic victims — iron rusts, copper turns green, silver tarnishes. All of this is corrosion.
  • Common agents that corrode things include water, oxygen, acids, salt, moisture, chemicals, and pollutants.
  • Common materials that corrode include iron, steel, copper, zinc, aluminum, and other metals. However, certain materials like plastics and some alloys are specifically valued because they resist corrosion.

Note: Not all materials corrode. Wood rots, rubber degrades, glass weathers — but "corrode" is used specifically when a chemical reaction is the mechanism of destruction. It is most accurately applied to metals.
The Figurative Meaning (Just as Important)

"Corrode" is used powerfully in non-physical, figurative contexts to describe the slow, invisible destruction of something abstract — a relationship, a society, a person's character, an institution, etc.

Just as acid eats away iron from the outside, abstract forces can slowly eat away at good things:

"Years of lies had corroded the trust between them."
"Corruption corrodes democracy from within."
"Bitterness, if left unchecked, will corrode the soul."
"Poverty and neglect corroded the community over generations."

In all these cases, the idea is the same: something destructive is working slowly, from the inside or the outside, weakening and hollowing out something that was once strong. The damage builds invisibly until it becomes impossible to ignore.

This figurative use is extremely common in formal writing, journalism, literature, and speech — so knowing it is essential.
Common Collocations (Words That Go With "Corrode")

These are the words you will frequently see paired with "corrode" in natural usage:

  • Slowly corrode — emphasizing the gradual nature
  • Gradually corrode — same idea
  • Begin to corrode — the early stage
  • Corrode rapidly / quickly — when the process is accelerated
  • Corrode from within — often figurative, meaning the destruction is internal and hidden
  • Corrode over time — highlighting the time element
Related Word Forms

Since you need the full picture, here are the other forms of this word:

  • Corroded (adjective / past tense verb) — already damaged by corrosion. "The corroded pipes finally burst."
  • Corroding (present participle) — currently in the process. "The corroding metal smells faintly of rust."
  • Corrosion (noun) — the process or result of corroding. "The bridge was weakened by decades of corrosion."
  • Corrosive (adjective) — describing something that has the ability to corrode. "Acid is highly corrosive." Also used figuratively: "a corrosive influence on young minds."
Synonyms — and How They Differ

Understanding where "corrode" stands among similar words will sharpen your understanding:

  • Erode — wearing away by physical force (wind, water, friction). A river erodes a riverbank physically. Acid corrodes metal chemically. The boundary blurs in figurative use, and both can be used loosely.
  • Rust — a specific type of corrosion that applies only to iron and steel. All rusting is corroding, but not all corroding is rusting.
  • Decay — a broader word for breaking down; applies to organic matter (food, wood, flesh) and does not require a chemical reaction in the strict chemical sense.
  • Deteriorate — to get worse gradually; very general and not specific to chemical reactions or physical surfaces.
  • Eat away at — a phrase that captures the informal spirit of corroding. Often used figuratively. "Guilt ate away at him."

Corrode is the precise, formal, and accurate word when you want to name the chemical destruction of a material — and the most vivid figurative word when you want to describe slow, hidden destruction of something abstract.
Putting It All Together — Rich Example Sentences

Here are varied sentences that show the full range of the word:

  1. The battery leaked and corroded the metal contacts inside the device.
  2. Iron will begin to corrode within hours if submerged in saltwater.
  3. The ancient coins were corroded beyond recognition.
  4. Without proper maintenance, the steel framework will corrode over time.
  5. Suspicion and jealousy had quietly corroded what was once a great friendship.
  6. Propaganda corrodes the public's ability to think critically.
  7. The pipes beneath the city had been corroding for thirty years before anyone noticed.
  8. A single dishonest act can begin to corrode a person's integrity.
The One-Sentence Summary

If you had to remember just one thing: to corrode is to slowly and chemically destroy something from the surface or from within — whether that something is a metal pipe or a person's trust in a friend.
